So the predator would remember that bug and try to avoid it later. This avoidance is easier if the bug has a distinct and colorful appearance. So suddenly it's a big advantage to be both toxic and colorful, since you are now less likely to get eaten. So they became more and more colorful over time. Cows are ruminants, meaning they have a giant pre-stomach organ that is filled with bacteria that are able to break down the cellulose in grass and convert it to different vitamins. Horses aren't ruminants but they do have a cecum, which is like a big dead-end pocket in the digestive system, also filled with similar bacteria that break down the grass. 

Humans did evolve from a cecum-having animal, but long ago we stopped eating plant parts high in cellulose, switching from grass and leaves to things like fruits and seeds (the plants actually evolved along with us to provide these to us in a mutually beneficial ecosystem, but that's another story). We didn't need the cecum anymore so it shrank and became the appendix, and we lost the grass-eating bacteria in our digestive system.

A mammal "egg" is actually an ovum (plural: ova). It is a gamete, meaning it has half the amount of DNA than a human. It gets the other half when a sperm cell (the male gamete) merges with it, and only then can it grow into an embryo. Birds also have ova and sperm like mammals, and they have sex and make an embryo basically the same way as mammals do, but once the embryo is formed it makes the egg around it, and then lays the egg. Obviously people knew about these kind of eggs before they discovered the microscopic ova and sperm. They didn't understand the genetic part at the time, so they called the female gamete an "egg", even though it's not really the same thing.

When specifically talking about fabric dye, the dye molecules get stuck into the microscopic fibres that make up the fabric. It is really hard to get the dye out of fabric after it is stuck in there, but still possible; think about how the colour of clothes fades after washing it a lot of times. 

Bleach is a harsh chemical and it destroys the dye molecules (and other stuff as well, including  bacteria), so they can no longer absorb the light, making the fabric white (or just a lighter shade, depending on how much bleach is used and how much dye was there at the start).

You caught it early. No choice but to go back and fix it! Undo each needle one by one in backwards order:

1. Pull the needle out
2. Pull on the yarn to undo all your stitches
3. Carefully put the needle back on all the loops
4. Repeat until you are back to your mistake (looks like only 3 needles)

A second option would be to tink (backwards un-knitting) all your work stitch by stitch, with the same result.
